Lemma 4.65
.

Suppose
\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)
with
d(\mathsf{t})=s_{r}s_{r+1}\ldots s_{n-2}
, and
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{n-1}
is not standard. Then
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
.

Proof.

As
d(\mathsf{t})
is the standard expression, we have
w_{n}=s_{r}s_{r+1}\ldots s_{n-2}
and
w_{n-1}=\ldots w_{1}=1
. Write
\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)})
and
\lambda^{(\ell)}=(\lambda^{(\ell)}_{1},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k})
, as
\mathsf{t}=\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}{\cdot}w_{n}
, we have
\mathsf{t}^{-1}(n)=(k,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)
. By (
2.29
) we have

\mathsf{t}^{-1}(k)=\begin{cases}(\mathsf{t}^{\lambda})^{-1}(k+1),&\text{ if $r\leq k\leq n-2$,}\\
(\mathsf{t}^{\lambda})^{-1}(r),&\text{ if $k=n-1$,}\\
(\mathsf{t}^{\lambda})^{-1}(k),&\text{ otherwise.}\end{cases}

As
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{n-1}
is not standard,
n-1
and
n
are adjacent in
\mathsf{t}
. So in
r
and
n
are adjacent in
\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}
. But
r\leq n-2
. Hence
r
has to be on the above of
n
in
\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}
. i.e.
(\mathsf{t}^{\lambda})^{-1}(r)=\mathsf{t}^{-1}(n-1)=(k-1,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)
. This shows that
\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k-1}=\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k}
and
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
. ∎

Example 4.66
.

Suppose
\lambda=(4,3,3)
and
\mathsf{t}=\mbox{\tiny$\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\vbox{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$3$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$4$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$5$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$6$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$9$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$8$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$9$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$10$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt$}\,
. Therefore
d(\mathsf{t})=s_{7}s_{8}
and
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{9}
is not standard. Notice that
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
.

Recall that we have a standard expression for
d(\mathsf{t})
such that
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{1}
, where
w_{i}=1
or
w_{i}=s_{a_{i}}s_{a_{i}+1}\ldots s_{i-1}
for
1\leq a_{i}\leq i-1
and
1\leq i\leq n
.

Lemma 4.67
.

Suppose
\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)
and
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{1}
is the standard expression where
w_{i}\neq 1
if
i\geq r+2
or
i=r
and
w_{i}=1
if
i<r
or
i=r+1
, i.e.
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{r+2}w_{r}
. If
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}
is not standard, then
l(w_{i})\geq l(w_{r})+1
for
i\geq r+2
.

Proof.

Write
\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)})
and
\lambda^{(\ell)}=(\lambda^{(\ell)}_{1},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k})
. Because
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}
is not standard,
r
and
r+1
are adjacent in
\mathsf{t}
. By (
2.29
), as
w_{i}\neq 1
for
i\geq r+2

(k,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)=(\mathsf{t}^{(n+1)})^{-1}(n)=(\mathsf{t}^{(n)})^{-1}(n-1)=\ldots=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+3)})^{-1}(r+2)=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)})^{-1}(r+1).

Notice that
w_{r+1}=1
and
w_{r}
doesn’t involve
s_{r}
or
s_{r+1}
, we have

(k,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)})^{-1}(r+1)=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+1)})^{-1}(r+1)=(\mathsf{t}^{(r)})^{-1}(r+1).

Since
w_{r}\neq 1
and
w_{r+1}=1
, recall
w_{r}=s_{a_{r}}s_{a_{r}+1}\ldots s_{r-2}s_{r-1}
, by (
2.29
) we have

(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)})^{-1}(a_{r})=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+1)})^{-1}(a_{r})=(\mathsf{t}^{(r)})^{-1}(r).

Since
w_{i}=1
for
i<r
, we have
\mathsf{t}^{(r)}=\mathsf{t}
. Then
\mathsf{t}^{-1}(r+1)=(k,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)
. Because
a_{r}\leq r-1<r+1
, by (
2.29
),
a_{r}
is not on the left of
r+1
in
\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)}
because
\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)}|_{r+1}=\mathsf{t}^{\mu}
with
\mu=\Shape(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)}|_{r+1})
. As
r
and
r+1
are adjacent in
\mathsf{t}
and
(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)})^{-1}(a_{r})=(\mathsf{t}^{(r)})^{-1}(r)=\mathsf{t}^{-1}(r)
, we must have
\mathsf{t}^{-1}(r)=(k-1,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)
. Therefore by the definition of the standard expression, we have
l(w_{r})=\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k}-1
.

Since
(k,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k},\ell)=(\mathsf{t}^{(n+1)})^{-1}(n)=(\mathsf{t}^{(n)})^{-1}(n-1)=\ldots=(\mathsf{t}^{(r+2)})^{-1}(r+1)
and (
2.29
), we have
l(w_{i})\geq\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k}=l(w_{r})+1
for all
i\geq r+2
. ∎

Lemma 4.68
.

Suppose
\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)
and
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{1}
with
w_{i}\neq 1
if
i>r+2
or
i=r
and
w_{i}=1
if
i<r
or
i=r+1
. If
l(w_{i})=l(w_{r})+1
for all
i\geq r+2
, i.e.
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{r+2}w_{r}
, and
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}
is not standard, then
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
.

Proof.

Write
\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)})
and
\lambda^{(\ell)}=(\lambda^{(\ell)}_{1},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k})
. From the proof of
subsection 4.5
we have seen that
l(w_{i})=\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k}
for
i\geq r+2
and
l(w_{r})=\lambda^{(\ell)}_{k}-1
. Therefore if
\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}(k-1,\lambda_{k-1}^{(\ell)},\ell)=t
,

\begin{cases}w_{n}=s_{t}s_{t+1}\ldots s_{n-1},&\\
w_{n-1}=s_{t-1}s_{t}\ldots s_{n-2},&\\
\ldots\ldots\ldots&\\
w_{r+2}=s_{t-n+r+2}s_{t-n+r+3}\ldots s_{r+1},&\\
w_{r}=s_{t-n+r+1}s_{t-n+r+2}\ldots s_{r-1},\end{cases}

and by direct calculation we see that such
d(\mathsf{t})
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
.∎

Example 4.69
.

Suppose
\lambda=(7,5,3)
and
\mathsf{t}=\mbox{\tiny$\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\vbox{\vbox{\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$1$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$2$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$3$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$4$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$5$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$6$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$7$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$8$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$9$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$12$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$14$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$15$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt\moveright 0.0pt\vbox{\hrule height=0.3pt\hbox{\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$10$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$11$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt\hbox to5.4381pt{\hfil$13$\hfil}\vrule height=4.35048pt,width=0.3pt,depth=1.0876pt}\hrule height=0.3pt}\vskip-0.3pt}}\hskip 0.0pt$}\,
. Then

d(\mathsf{t})=s_{12}s_{13}s_{14}{\cdot}s_{11}s_{12}s_{13}{\cdot}s_{10}s_{11}.

So we can write
d(\mathsf{t})=w_{15}w_{14}w_{13}w_{12}
where
w_{15}=s_{12}s_{13}s_{14}
,
w_{14}=s_{11}s_{12}s_{13}
,
w_{13}=1
and
w_{12}=s_{10}s_{11}
. Notice
l(w_{15})=l(w_{14})=l(w_{12})+1
and
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{12}
is not standard, and furthermore,
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
.

Finally we are ready to prove the most important result of this subsection.

Proposition 4.70
.

Suppose
\lambda\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
and that
\mathsf{t}
is a standard
\lambda
-tableau such that
l(d(\mathsf{t}))\leq m_{\lambda}
and
d(\mathsf{t}){\cdot}s_{r}
is not reduced or
\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}
is not standard for some
r
. Then

\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}=\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}.

for any standard
\lambda
-tableau
\mathsf{s}
.

Proof.

First we set
\mathsf{s}=\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}
. By the definition of
m_{\lambda}
the Proposition holds when
l(d(\mathsf{t}))<m_{\lambda}
. Hence we only have to consider the case when
l(d(\mathsf{t}))=m_{\lambda}
. By
subsection 4.1
we have
l(d(\mathsf{t}))>0
. Therefore
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\neq 1
.

Recall that the standard expression of
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}
has the form
\psi_{w_{n}}\psi_{w_{n-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{2}}
where
\psi_{w_{i}}=\psi_{a_{i}}\psi_{a_{i}+1}\psi_{a_{i}+2}\ldots\psi_{i-1}
for some
a_{i}\leq i-1
or
\psi_{w_{i}}=1
. Let
k
be the smallest positive integer such that
\psi_{w_{k}}\neq 1
and
\psi_{w_{i}}=1
for all
i<k
. Because
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\neq 1
, the integer
k
is well-defined. So
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}=\psi_{w_{n}}\psi_{w_{n-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k}}
.

Recall that by
subsection 4.5
and
4.5
, if
d(\mathsf{t})
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I or type II, we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

We separate the problem into several cases:

Case
4.5
a
:
k-1\not\in\{r-1,r,r+1\}
. Then

\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}=\psi_{w_{n}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k}}=\psi_{w_{n}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k+1}}\psi_{a_{k}}\psi_{a_{k}+1}\ldots\psi_{k-2}\psi_{k-1}.

In this case
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I. Therefore by
subsection 4.5
,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

Case
4.5
b
:
k-1=r
. Define
\mathsf{w}=\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}
. Hence
d(\mathsf{t})=d(\mathsf{w}){\cdot}s_{r}
. Write
\mathbf{i}_{\mathsf{w}}=(i_{1}i_{2}\ldots i_{n})
.

e_{\lambda}y_{\lambda}\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}=y_{\lambda}\psi_{d(\mathsf{w})}e(\mathbf{i}_{\mathsf{w}})\psi_{r}^{2}=\begin{cases}0,&\text{ if $i_{r}=i_{r+1}$,}\\
y_{\lambda}\psi_{d(\mathsf{w})}e(\mathbf{i}_{\mathsf{w}})=\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{w}},&\text{ if $|i_{r}-i_{r+1}|>1$,}\\
\pm\ y_{\lambda}\psi_{d(\mathsf{w})}e(\mathbf{i}_{\mathsf{w}})(y_{r}-y_{r+1})\\
\hskip 28.45274pt=\pm\ \psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{w}}(y_{r}-y_{r+1}),&\text{ if $i_{r}=i_{r+1}\pm 1$.}\end{cases}

By
subsection 4.2
we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

Case
4.5
c
:
k-1=r+1
.

4.5
c.1:

\psi_{w_{i}}=1
for some
i>k
and
i\neq n
. Then we have

\displaystyle\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\psi_{w_{n}}\psi_{w_{n-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{i+2}}\psi_{w_{i+1}}\psi_{w_{i-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k}}\psi_{r}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\psi_{w_{n}}\psi_{w_{n-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{i+2}}(\psi_{a_{i+1}}\psi_{a_{i+1}+1}\ldots\psi_{i-1}\psi_{i})\psi_{w_{i-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k}}\psi_{r}.

As
i>k=r+2>r+1
, we have

\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}=(\psi_{w_{n}}\psi_{w_{n-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{i+2}}\psi_{a_{i+1}}\psi_{a_{i+1}+1}\ldots\psi_{i-1}\psi_{w_{i-1}}\ldots\psi_{w_{k}}\psi_{i})\psi_{r},

which shows that
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I. By
subsection 4.5
we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
c.2:

\psi_{w_{n}}=1
. In this case
\psi_{n-1}
is not involved in
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}
. By
subsection 4.3
we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
c.3:

\psi_{w_{i}}\neq 1
for
i>k
and
l(\psi_{w_{k}})>1
. Then we see that
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type II. By
subsection 4.5
we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
c.4:

\psi_{w_{i}}\neq 1
for
i>k
, and there exists
k<j<n
such that
l(\psi_{w_{k}})=l(\psi_{w_{k+1}})=\ldots=l(\psi_{w_{j-1}})=1
and
l(\psi_{w_{j}})>1
. Then we have

w_{j}{\cdot}w_{j-1}=s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-3}s_{j-2}s_{j-1}{\cdot}s_{j-2}=s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-3}{\cdot}s_{j-1}s_{j-2}s_{j-1}.

Therefore

\displaystyle d(\mathsf{t})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-3}{\cdot}s_{j-1}s_{j-2}s_{j-1}{\cdot}w_{j-2}\ldots w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+1}s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-3}{\cdot}s_{j-1}s_{j-2}w_{j-2}\ldots w_{k}{\cdot}s_{j-1},

and
j-1\geq k=r+2>r+1
,
s_{j-1}
and
s_{r}
commute, which shows that
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I. By
subsection 4.5
, we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
c.5:

l(\psi_{w_{k}})=l(\psi_{w_{k+1}})=\ldots=l(\psi_{w_{n}})=1
. Then by
subsection 4.5
,
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
. Hence by
subsection 4.4
,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

Case
4.5
d
:
k-1=r-1
.

4.5
d.1:

\psi_{w_{k+1}}\neq 1
. Then

\displaystyle d(\mathsf{t})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{k+2}{\cdot}w_{k+1}w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{k+2}{\cdot}s_{a_{k+1}}s_{a_{k+1}+1}\ldots s_{k-1}s_{k}{\cdot}s_{a_{k}}s_{a_{k}+1}\ldots s_{k-2}s_{k-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{k+2}s_{a_{k+1}}s_{a_{k+1}+1}\ldots s_{k-1}s_{a_{k}}s_{a_{k}+1}\ldots s_{k-2}{\cdot}s_{k}s_{k-1},

and as
r=k
, we see that
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type II. Therefore
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
by
subsection 4.5
.

4.5
d.2:

k=n-1
and
\psi_{w_{k+1}}=\psi_{w_{n}}=1
. The
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}=\psi_{w_{n-1}}\psi_{n-1}=\psi_{a_{n-1}}\psi_{a_{n-1}+1}\ldots\psi_{n-2}\psi_{n-1}
. Then by
subsection 4.5
,
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
. Hence by
subsection 4.4
,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}^{\lambda}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
d.3:

k<n-1
,
\psi_{w_{k+1}}=1
and
\psi_{w_{n}}=1
. Then
n-1>k=r
. So
\psi_{d(\mathsf{t})}\psi_{r}
doesn’t involve
\psi_{n-1}
. By
subsection 4.3
we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
d.4:

k<n-1
,
\psi_{w_{k+1}}=1
and there exists
k+1<j<n
such that
\psi_{w_{j}}=1
and
\psi_{w_{j+1}}\neq 1
. In this case we have

\displaystyle d(\mathsf{t})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+2}w_{j+1}w_{j}w_{j-1}\ldots w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+2}{\cdot}s_{a_{j+1}}s_{a_{j+1}+1}\ldots s_{j-1}s_{j}{\cdot}w_{j-1}\ldots w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+2}{\cdot}s_{a_{j+1}}s_{a_{j+1}+1}\ldots s_{j-1}{\cdot}w_{j-1}\ldots w_{k}){\cdot}s_{j}.

As
j>k+1=r+1
,
\psi_{j}
and
\psi_{r}
commute. Therefore
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I. By
subsection 4.5
, we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
d.5:

k<n-1
,
\psi_{w_{k+1}}=1
and for any
j>k+1
,
\psi_{w_{j}}\neq 1
. Then by
subsection 4.5
, we have
l(\psi_{w_{j}})\geq l(\psi_{w_{k}})+1
for all
j\geq k+2
.

4.5
d.5.1:
Suppose
l(\psi_{w_{k+2}})>l(\psi_{w_{k}})+1
. So we have
a_{k+2}\leq a_{k}
, and therefore

\displaystyle w_{k+2}w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle s_{a_{k+2}}s_{a_{k+2}+1}\ldots s_{k}s_{k+1}{\cdot}s_{a_{k}}s_{a_{k}+1}\ldots s_{k-2}s_{k-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle s_{a_{k}+1}\ldots s_{k-1}s_{k}{\cdot}s_{a_{k+2}}s_{a_{k+2}+1}\ldots s_{k}s_{k+1}.

Therefore

\displaystyle d(\mathsf{t})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{k+3}{\cdot}w_{k+2}w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}w_{k+3}{\cdot}s_{a_{k}+1}\ldots s_{k-1}s_{k}{\cdot}s_{a_{k+2}}s_{a_{k+2}+1}\ldots s_{k}s_{k+1}.

Then because
k=r
,
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type II. Therefore, by
subsection 4.5
,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
d.5.2:
There exists
j>k+2
such that
l(\psi_{w_{k+2}})=l(\psi_{w_{k+3}})=\ldots=l(\psi_{w_{j-1}})=l(\psi_{w_{k}})+1
and
l(\psi_{w_{j}})>l(\psi_{w_{k}})+1
. So we have
l(\psi_{w_{j}})>l(\psi_{w_{j-1}})
and
a_{j}\leq a_{j-1}
, and therefore

\displaystyle w_{j}w_{j-1}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-2}s_{j-1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j-1}}s_{a_{j-1}+1}\ldots s_{j-3}s_{j-2}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle s_{a_{j-1}+1}\ldots s_{j-2}s_{j-1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j}}s_{a_{j}+1}\ldots s_{j-2}s_{j-1}.

Therefore

\displaystyle d(\mathsf{t})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+1}w_{j}w_{j-1}w_{j-2}\ldots w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j-1}+1}\ldots s_{j-1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j}}\ldots s_{j-2}s_{j-1}{\cdot}w_{j-2}\ldots w_{k}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(w_{n}w_{n-1}\ldots w_{j+1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j-1}+1}\ldots s_{j-1}{\cdot}s_{a_{j}}\ldots s_{j-2}{\cdot}w_{j-2}\ldots w_{k}){\cdot}s_{j-1}.

Then because
j-1>k+1=r+1
,
s_{j-1}
and
s_{r}
commutes. Hence
\mathsf{t}
is unlocked by
s_{r}
in type I and therefore, by
subsection 4.5
,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

4.5
d.5.3:

l(\psi_{w_{k+2}})=l(\psi_{w_{k+3}})=\ldots=l(\psi_{w_{n-1}})=l(\psi_{w_{k}})+1
. By
subsection 4.5
,
\mathsf{t}
is the last Garnir tableau of shape
\lambda
. By
subsection 4.4
, we have
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
.

By the above cases,
\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}
is always in
R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
. Therefore by
subsection 2.4
, we have

\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}=\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{t}^{\lambda},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}=\sum_{\mathsf{v}\rhd t}c_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{v}}+\sum_{\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(>\lambda)}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}.

Giving any standard
\lambda
-tableau
\mathsf{s}
, we have
\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}=\psi^{*}_{d(\mathsf{s})}\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}
. Notice
\psi_{d(\mathsf{s})}^{*}\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{v}}=\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{v}}
. For any
\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(>\lambda)
,
\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\in R^{>\lambda}_{n}
. As
\lambda\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
, by
subsection 3.1
,
R^{>\lambda}_{n}
is an ideal. Therefore
\psi^{*}_{d(\mathsf{s})}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\in R^{>\lambda}_{n}
. These arguments yield that
\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}\in R^{\geq\lambda}_{n}
. By
subsection 2.4
we completes the proof.∎

The following Corollary is straightforward by
subsection 4.2
and
subsection 4.5
.

Corollary 4.71
.

Suppose
\lambda\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
, for any standard
\lambda
-tableau
\mathsf{t}
with
l(d(\mathsf{t}))\leq m_{\lambda}
, then

\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}=\begin{cases}\psi_{\mathsf{t}^{\lambda}\mathsf{w}}+\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}},&\text{ if $\mathsf{w}=\mathsf{u}{\cdot}s_{r}$ is standard and $d(\mathsf{u}){\cdot}s_{r}$ is reduced,}\\
\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}},&\text{ if $\mathsf{u}{\cdot}s_{r}$ is not standard or $d(\mathsf{u}){\cdot}s_{r}$ is not reduced.}\end{cases}

for any standard
\lambda
-tableau
\mathsf{s}
.

4.6. Integral basis Theorem

In this subsection we will complete the main Theorem of this paper.

Theorem 4.72
.

Suppose
\lambda\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
, we have
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{I}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{y}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{\psi}
.

Proof.

By
subsection 3.1
we have when
\lambda\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
then
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{I}
. By
subsection 4.1
, we have
0<m_{\lambda}
, i.e.
1\leq m_{\lambda}
. Assume
l=l(d(\mathsf{u})
for some
\mathsf{u}\in\Std(\lambda)
, by
subsection 4.2
and
subsection 4.5
, for any
\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)
with
l(d(\mathsf{t}))=l
, we have

\displaystyle\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}y_{r}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}},

\displaystyle\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{r}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\begin{cases}\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{w}}+\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}},&\text{ if $\mathsf{w}=\mathsf{t}{\cdot}s_{r}$ is standard and $d(\mathsf{u}){\cdot}s_{r}$ is reduced,}\\
\sum_{(\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v})\rhd(\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t})}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}},&\text{ if $\mathsf{u}{\cdot}s_{r}$ is not standard or $d(\mathsf{u}){\cdot}s_{r}$ is not reduced.}\end{cases}

This implies that
l<m_{\lambda}
, i.e.
l+1\leq m_{\lambda}
. So by induction, for any
\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)
, we have
l(d(\mathsf{t}))<m_{\lambda}
. Therefore
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{y}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{\psi}
. This completes the proof.∎

Theorem 4.73
.

The set
\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{st}^{\mathbb{Z}}}\mid{\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda)\text{ for $\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}$}}\,\}}
is a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda}(\mathbb{Z})
.

Proof.

It’s trivial that when
n=1
the Theorem holds. Assume for any
n^{\prime}<n
the Theorem follows. Suppose we can write all multipartitions of
n
as
\lambda_{[1]},\lambda_{[2]},\ldots,\lambda_{[k]}
where
\lambda_{[1]}>\lambda_{[2]}>\ldots>\lambda_{[k]}
. As
\lambda_{[1]}=((n),\emptyset,\ldots,\emptyset)
, by
subsection 3.1
,
subsection 3.1
and
3.1
, we have
\lambda_{[1]}\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{I}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{y}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{\psi}
. Hence
\lambda_{[2]}\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
. Now assume
\lambda_{[i]}\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
, by
subsection 4.6
,
\lambda_{[i]}\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{I}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{y}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{\psi}
. Hence
\lambda_{[i+1]}\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
. Therefore for any
i
,
\lambda_{[i]}\in\mathscr{S}_{n}^{\Lambda}
. Hence, for any
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
,
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{I}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{y}\cap\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{\psi}
. Recall that

R^{\Lambda}_{n}=\{r\in\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda}(\mathbb{Z})\ |\ r=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\mu)\\
\mu\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}\end{subarray}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}},c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\in\mathbb{Z}\}.

So
R^{\Lambda}_{n}
is an ideal.

Now, for any
\mathbf{i}=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{n})\in I^{n}
, set
\mathbf{j}=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{n-1})\in I^{n-1}
. Because
e(\mathbf{j})\in\mathscr{R}_{n-1}^{\Lambda}
, by assumption we have
e(\mathbf{j})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n-1}\\
\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\mu)\end{subarray}}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\in R_{n-1}^{\Lambda}
and hence that
e(\mathbf{i})=\theta_{i_{n}}(e(\mathbf{j}))=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n-1}\\
\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\mu)\end{subarray}}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\theta_{i_{n}}(\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}})
.

For any
\mu\in\mathscr{P}_{n-1}^{\Lambda}
and
\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\mu)
, we have

\theta_{i_{n}}(\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}})=\psi^{*}_{d(\mathsf{u})}e(\mathbf{i}_{\mu}\vee i_{n})y_{\mu}\psi_{d(\mathsf{v})}.

By
subsection 3.1
and
subsection 3.1
, we have
e(\mathbf{i}_{\mu}\vee i_{n})y_{\mu}y_{n}^{0}\in R_{n}^{\Lambda}
. Then because
R^{\Lambda}_{n}
is an ideal,

e(\mathbf{i})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mu\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n-1}\\
\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\mu)\end{subarray}}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\theta_{i_{n}}(\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}})\in R^{\Lambda}_{n}.

Then we have
R^{\Lambda}_{n}=\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda}(\mathbb{Z})
. By
subsection 2.4
, the set
\{\psi_{st}^{\mathbb{Z}}\ |\ \mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\text{Std}(\lambda)\text{ for $\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}$}\}
is linearly independent. Hence,
\{\psi_{st}^{\mathbb{Z}}\ |\ \mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\text{Std}(\lambda)\text{ for $\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}$}\}
is a basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda}(\mathbb{Z})
.

By definition, the elements of the set are homogeneous. That this basis is cellular is trivial by
subsection 2.4
and
subsection 2.4
. This completes the proof.∎

The next Corollary is a straightforward application of
subsection 4.6
.

Corollary 4.74
.

For any
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
,
e(\mathbf{i})\neq 0
if and only if
\mathbf{i}
is the residue sequence of a standard tableau
\mathsf{t}
.

Proof.

Suppose
\mathbf{i}
is the residue sequence of a standard tableau
\mathsf{t}
. By
subsection 4.6
we have
\psi^{\mathbb{Z}}_{\mathsf{t}\mathsf{t}}\neq 0
. Because
\psi^{\mathbb{Z}}_{\mathsf{t}\mathsf{t}}=\psi^{\mathbb{Z}}_{\mathsf{t}\mathsf{t}}e(\mathbf{i})
, we must have
e(\mathbf{i})\neq 0
.

Suppose
\mathbf{i}
is not the residue sequence of any standard tableau. By
subsection 4.6
we can write

1=\sum_{\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi^{\mathbb{Z}}_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}},

and hence
e(\mathbf{i})=1{\cdot}e(\mathbf{i})=\sum_{\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi^{\mathbb{Z}}_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}e(\mathbf{i})=0
, which completes the proof. ∎

5. A new basis of the Affine KLR Algebras

In
subsection 4.6
we have shown that
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})
is a
\mathbb{Z}
-free algebra with basis
\{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\ |\ \mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda),\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}\}
. In this section we extend this result and construct a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})
. Moreover, for any weight
\Lambda
we obtain a homogeneous basis of the ideal
N_{n}^{\Lambda}
as a subset of the graded cellular basis of
R_{n}(\mathbb{Z})
. As an application we obtain a new classification of the complete set of simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules by using the graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
. Unlike in previous sections, this section laces no constraints upon
e
as we now allow the case
e=2
.

5.1. Infinite sequence of weights and basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}

This subsection introduces a special kind of sequences of weights
\Lambda^{\infty}
. We use these infinite sequences of weights to define a graded cellular basis for
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
by combining the graded cellular basis of the algebras
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
.

We fix an integer
e\geq 0
and
e\neq 1
, and consider the KLR algebras
\mathscr{R}_{n}=\mathscr{R}_{n}(\mathbb{Z})
. Suppose
\Lambda=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}\Lambda_{i}
and
\Lambda^{\prime}=\sum_{i\in I}a^{\prime}_{i}\Lambda_{i}
are two weights in
P_{+}
. Define a partial ordering on
P^{+}
and write
\Lambda\leq\Lambda^{\prime}
if
a_{i}\leq a_{i}^{\prime}
for all
i\in I
. Write
\Lambda<\Lambda^{\prime}
if
\Lambda\leq\Lambda^{\prime}
and
\Lambda\neq\Lambda^{\prime}
.

Definition 5.1
.

Suppose
\Lambda^{\infty}=(\Lambda^{(k)})_{k\geq 1}
is a sequence of weights in
P^{+}
where
\Lambda^{(k)}=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}^{(k)}\Lambda_{i}
. It is an
increasing sequence
if
\Lambda^{(k)}<\Lambda^{(k+1)}
for all
k\geq 1
. The sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
is called
standard
if
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}a_{i}^{(k)}=\infty
, for all
i\in I
.

Example 5.2
.

Suppose
e>0
. Let
\Lambda^{\infty}
be any increasing sequence of weights such that
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda_{1}
and
\Lambda^{(k)}=\Lambda^{(k-1)}+\Lambda_{i}
whenever
k\equiv i\pmod{e}
. For example, when
e=3
, we have

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(1)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(2)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{2},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(3)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{2}+\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(4)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\Lambda_{1}+\Lambda_{2}+\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(5)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\Lambda_{1}+2\Lambda_{2}+\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(6)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2\Lambda_{1}+2\Lambda_{2}+2\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(7)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 3\Lambda_{1}+2\Lambda_{2}+2\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\ldots\ldots

\displaystyle\ldots

\displaystyle\ldots\ldots\ldots

So in this case we have
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}a_{i}^{(k)}=\infty
for any
i\in I
and
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence.

Example 5.3
.

Suppose
e=0
. Define
\Lambda^{\infty}
where
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda_{0}
and
\Lambda^{(k)}=\Lambda^{(k-1)}+\Lambda_{i}
with
i=(k-1)-(n-1)^{2}-(n-1)=k-n^{2}+n-1
if

. In more details,

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(1)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(2)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-1}+\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(3)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-1}+2\Lambda_{0},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(4)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-1}+2\Lambda_{0}+\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(5)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-2}+\Lambda_{-1}+2\Lambda_{0}+\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(6)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-2}+2\Lambda_{-1}+2\Lambda_{0}+\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(7)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\Lambda_{-2}+2\Lambda_{-1}+3\Lambda_{0}+\Lambda_{1},

\displaystyle\Lambda^{(8)}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle\ldots\ldots

\displaystyle\ldots

So in this case we have
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}a_{i}^{(k)}=\infty
for any
i\in I
and
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence.

Recall that for any weight
\Lambda=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}\Lambda_{i}
, we can define the two-sided ideal
N_{n}^{\Lambda}
of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
. The ideal
N_{n}^{\Lambda}
is generated by elements
e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}}
for all
\mathbf{i}=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{n})\in I^{n}
. By definition,
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}\cong\mathscr{R}_{n}/N_{n}^{\Lambda}
. There is a natural injective homomorphism sending
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
to
\mathscr{R}_{n}
by sending
e(\mathbf{i})
,
y_{r}
and
\psi_{r}
to
\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})
,
\hat{y}_{r}
and
\hat{\psi}_{r}
, respectively. Hence we can consider
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
as a
\mathbb{Z}
-submodule of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
and write
\mathscr{R}_{n}\cong\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}\oplus N_{n}^{\Lambda}
as
\mathbb{Z}
-modules.

Recall
Q_{+}=\sum_{i\in I}\mathbb{N}\alpha_{i}
is defined in subsection 1.1. For
\alpha=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}\alpha_{i}\in Q_{+}
, define
|\alpha|=\sum_{\T1\i\in I}a_{i}
. Then for any
\alpha\in Q_{+}
with
|\alpha|=n
, define
I^{\alpha}
to be the set of all sequences
\mathbf{i}=(i_{1},i_{2},\ldots,i_{n})\in I^{n}
such that
a_{i}=|\mathinner{\{\,{1\leq r\leq n}\mid{i_{r}=i}\,\}}|
. By definition, if
\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j}\in I^{\alpha}
then there exists
v\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
such that
\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}{\cdot}v
. Define
\hat{e}_{\alpha}=\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\in\mathscr{R}_{n}
and
e_{\alpha}=\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}e(\mathbf{i})\in\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
.

The following result is trivial by the relations of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
.

Lemma 5.4
.

Suppose
\alpha,\beta\in Q_{+}
. Then
\mathscr{R}_{n}\hat{e}_{\alpha}\neq 0
and
\hat{e}_{\beta}\mathscr{R}_{n}\hat{e}_{\alpha}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\mathscr{R}_{n}e_{\alpha}=\delta_{\alpha\beta}\hat{e}_{\beta}\mathscr{R}_{n}
.

We then define
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}=\mathscr{R}_{n}\hat{e}_{\alpha}
,
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}=\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}e_{\alpha}
and
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}=N_{n}^{\Lambda}\hat{e}_{\alpha}
. We see that
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}\hat{e}(\mathbf{j})=0
if
\mathbf{j}\not\in I^{\alpha}
. Finally, because

\mathscr{R}_{n}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_{+}}\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}\hskip 14.22636pt\text{and}\hskip 14.22636pt\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_{+}}\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda},

and by the relations
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
and
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
’s are subalgebras of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
and
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
, respectively. Hence we will mainly work in
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
,
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
and
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
and extend the basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
to
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
and hence generate a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
.

By
subsection 4.6
and the orthogonality of
e(\mathbf{i})
’s we can give a basis for
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

Proposition 5.5
.

Suppose
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
and
\Lambda\in P_{+}
. The set

\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}}\mid{\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n},\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda),\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}

is a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

5.2. Minimum degree of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}

Fix
\alpha\in Q_{+}
. In the last subsection we introduced a standard sequence of
\Lambda^{\infty}
. For each
k
and
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
, we define the
minimum degree
of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
to be the integer

m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\text{min}\{\deg(r)\ |\ \text{$r$ is a homogeneous element in $N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}$}\}.

We will prove that
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}\rightarrow\infty
with
k\rightarrow\infty
. This result is quite important in the next subsection because it will allow us to extend the basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
to
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
.

First we need to find a general description of the homogeneous elements of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

Lemma 5.6
.

For
\Lambda=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}\Lambda_{i}\in P_{+}
and
\alpha\in Q_{+}
, the ideal
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
is spanned by

\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}}f(y)\psi_{v}}\mid{u,v\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},f(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}],\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}.

Proof.

By the definition of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
, any element of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
can be written as linear combination of elements of the form

\psi_{u_{k}}f_{k}(y)\psi_{u_{k-1}}\ldots\psi_{u_{2}}f_{2}(y)\psi_{u_{1}}f_{1}(y)e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}}g_{1}(y)\psi_{v_{1}}g_{2}(y)\psi_{v_{2}}\ldots\psi_{v_{l-1}}g_{l}(y)\psi_{v_{l}},

(5.7)

where
u_{i},v_{i}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
,
\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}
and
f_{i}(y),g_{i}(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}]
. In the view of
subsection 4.2
and
[
5
, Proposition 2.5]
, every element in the form of (
5.7
) can be written as linear combination of terms of the form
\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}}f(y)\psi_{v}
’s. Hence
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
is spanned by the elements given in the statement of the Lemma. ∎

The next result is directly implied by the above Lemma.

Proposition 5.8
.

Suppose that
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence and
\alpha\in Q_{+}
. Then
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\infty
.

Proof.

By
subsection 5.2
, for any
k\geq 1
we have

m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\min\mathinner{\{\,{\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}}f(y)\psi_{v})}\mid{u,v\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},f(y)\in\mathbb{Z}[y_{1},y_{2},\ldots,y_{n}],\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}.

By definition,
\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}}f(y)\psi_{v})=\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i}))+\deg(y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}})+\deg(f(y))+\deg(\psi_{v}e(\mathbf{i}{\cdot}v))
. As
u
and
v
are reduced expressions of permutations in
\mathfrak{S}_{n}
,
l(u)\leq\frac{(n-1)n}{2}
, and
\deg(\psi_{r}e(\mathbf{i}))\geq-2
for any
\mathbf{i}
. Hence,
\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i}))\geq-(n-1)n
. By the same reasoning,
\deg(\psi_{v}e(\mathbf{i}{\cdot}v))\geq-(n-1)n
. Then as
\deg(f(y))\geq 0
, we have
\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}}f(y)\psi_{v})\geq-2(n-1)n+2a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}
.

Define
a_{\alpha}^{(k)}=\min_{\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}
. We have

\deg(\psi_{u}e(\mathbf{i})y_{1}^{a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}}f(y)\psi_{v})\geq-2(n-1)n+2a_{\alpha}^{(k)},

for any
u
,
v
and
f
. Therefore
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}\geq 2a_{\alpha}^{(k)}-2(n-1)n
.

Choose
\mathbf{j}\in I^{\alpha}
. By definition,
I^{\alpha}=\mathinner{\{\,{\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}}\mid{\mathbf{i}=\mathbf{j}{\cdot}v\text{ with }v\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}\,\}}
. Then
|I^{\alpha}|\leq|\mathfrak{S}_{n}|<\infty
. Then
a_{i_{1}}^{(k)}\rightarrow\infty
as
k\rightarrow\infty
for any
\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}
implies
a_{\alpha}^{(k)}\rightarrow\infty
as
k\rightarrow\infty
because
I^{\alpha}
is finite. Therefore
m^{\Lambda^{(k)}}_{\alpha}\rightarrow\infty
. ∎

Remark 5.9
.

That the set
I^{\alpha}
is finite is important in the proof of
subsection 5.2
. If it were possible for
I^{\alpha}
to be infinite then knowing that
a^{(k)}_{i_{1}}\rightarrow\infty
for all
i\in I^{\alpha}
is not strong enough to imply that
a_{\alpha}^{(k)}\rightarrow\infty
as
k\rightarrow\infty
.

5.3. A graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}

In this subsection we will prove the main result of this section. First we introduce a special kind of multicharge
\kappa
corresponding to a standard sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
. Then for any
\alpha\in Q_{+}
, we will find a graded cellular basis
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
that corresponds to
\kappa
.

Definition 5.10
.

Suppose
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence. An
inverse multicharge sequence
for
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a infinite sequence
\kappa=(\ldots,\kappa_{3},\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
such that for any
k\geq 1
, if
\ell_{k}=l(\Lambda^{(k)})
, then
\kappa_{\Lambda^{(k)}}=(\kappa_{\ell_{k}},\kappa_{\ell_{k}-1},\ldots,\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
is a multicharge corresponding to
\Lambda^{(k)}
.

Example 5.11
.

Suppose
e=3
. Using the standard sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
introduced in Example
5.1
, we define a multicharge
\kappa=(\ldots,\kappa_{3},\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
where
\kappa_{k}\equiv k\pmod{e}
for
k\geq 1
. We can write
\kappa=(\ldots,0,2,1,0,2,1,0,2,1,0,2,1)
, and we have

\displaystyle\kappa_{\Lambda^{(1)}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(1),

\displaystyle\kappa_{\Lambda^{(2)}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(2,1),

\displaystyle\kappa_{\Lambda^{(3)}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(0,2,1),

\displaystyle\kappa_{\Lambda^{(4)}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(1,0,2,1),

\displaystyle\kappa_{\Lambda^{(5)}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(2,1,0,2,1),

\displaystyle\ldots\ldots

\displaystyle\ldots

\displaystyle\ldots\ldots\ldots

All of these multicharges correspond to
\Lambda^{(k)}
.

Fix a standard sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
and an inverse multicharge sequence
\kappa
for
\Lambda^{\infty}
. An
affine multipartition
of
n
is an ordered sequence
\hat{\lambda}=(\ldots,\lambda^{(2)},\lambda^{(1)})
of partitions such that
\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}|\lambda^{(i)}|=n
. Let
\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
be the set of all affine multipartitions of
n
. We define
young diagram

[\hat{\lambda}]
and
standard affine tableau

\hat{\mathsf{s}}
for affine multipartitions in the same way as for multipartitions. Let
\Std(\hat{\lambda})
be the set of all standard affine tableaux of shape
\hat{\lambda}
.

Fix an inverse multicharge sequence
\kappa=(\ldots,\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
. For any
\ell>0
, let
(\kappa_{\ell},\ldots,\kappa_{1})
be a multicharge and
\Lambda
be the unique weight corresponds to
(\kappa_{\ell},\ldots,\kappa_{1})
. We define a map
p_{\ell}\,{:}\,\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
, sending
\hat{\lambda}=(\ldots,\lambda^{(2)},\lambda^{(1)})\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
to
\lambda=(\lambda^{(\ell)},\lambda^{(\ell-1)},\ldots,\lambda^{(2)},\lambda^{(1)})\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
.

Define the
level
of
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
to be
l(\hat{\lambda})=\ell
if
\lambda^{(\ell)}\neq\emptyset
and
\lambda^{(i)}=\emptyset
for
i>\ell
. Suppose
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
with level
\ell
and
\lambda=p_{\ell}(\hat{\lambda})
, define
q_{\ell}\,{:}\,\Std(\hat{\lambda})\!\longrightarrow\!\Std(\lambda)
sending
\hat{\mathsf{t}}=(\ldots,\mathsf{t}^{(2)},\mathsf{t}^{(1)})\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
to
\mathsf{t}=(\mathsf{t}^{(\ell)},\mathsf{t}^{(\ell-1)},\ldots,\mathsf{t}^{(1)})\in\Std(\lambda)
.

In order to simplify the notations, we write
\lambda=p_{\ell}(\hat{\lambda})
if
l(\hat{\lambda})=\ell
. Similarly, if
l(\hat{\lambda})=\ell
, for
\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
, we write
\mathsf{t}=q_{\ell}(\hat{\mathsf{t}})\in\Std(\lambda)
. Define the degree of each standard affine tableau to be
\deg(\hat{\mathsf{s}})=\deg(\mathsf{s})
and the residue sequence of the affine tableau
\res(\hat{\mathsf{s}})=\res(\mathsf{s})
.

Extend dominance ordering
\unrhd
and lexicographic ordering
\geq
to
\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
by defining
\hat{\lambda}\unrhd\hat{\mu}
if
l(\hat{\lambda})>l(\hat{\mu})
or
l(\hat{\lambda})=l(\hat{\mu})
and
\lambda\unrhd\mu
and
\hat{\lambda}\rhd\hat{\mu}
if
\hat{\lambda}\unrhd\hat{\mu}
and
\hat{\lambda}\neq\hat{\mu}
for
\hat{\lambda},\hat{\mu}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
. We define the lexicographic orderings on
\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
similarly.

Lemma 5.14
.

Suppose
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
and
\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
. Then
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}
are homogeneous elements of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
and
\deg(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}})=\deg(\hat{\mathsf{s}})+\deg(\hat{\mathsf{t}})
.

Fix
\alpha\in Q_{+}
, a standard sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
and an inverse multicharge sequence
\kappa
corresponding to
\Lambda^{\infty}
. Define a set of homogeneous elements of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
by

\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}=\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}}\mid{\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n},\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda}),\res(\hat{\mathsf{t}})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}.

Note that by definition
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
depends on the choice of
\kappa
and hence on
\Lambda^{\infty}
. Remarkably, the main results of this section are true for any inverse multicharge sequence corresponding to
\Lambda^{\infty}
.

Proposition 5.15
.

The set
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a homogeneous basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
.

Proof.

By
subsection 5.3
, all of the elements of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
are homogeneous. So we only have to prove that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
. First of all we show that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
spans
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
.

If
r\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
, then we can write
r
as a linear combination of homogeneous elements, i.e.
r=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}c_{i}r_{i}
, where
c_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}
,
\deg(r_{i})=i
and there are only finite many
i\in\mathbb{N}
with
c_{i}\neq 0
. So it is enough to prove that any homogeneous element
r\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
is a linear combination of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
.

For any
\Lambda<\Lambda^{\prime}
, it is obvious that
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\prime}}\subseteq N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
. Moreover,
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\prime}}
is a
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
-ideal of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
. Hence we can define an infinite filtration

\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}>N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(1)}}>N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(2)}}>N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(3)}}>\ldots.

By
subsection 5.2
,
\lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}m^{\Lambda^{(k)}}_{\alpha}=\infty
, so if
r\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
is homogeneous then there exists an integer
k(r)
such that
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}>\deg(r)
whenever
k>k(r)
. Fix
k>k(r)
and hence
r\not\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
.

By
subsection 5.1
, choosing a multicharge
\kappa
corresponding to
\Lambda
,
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}\cong\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}/N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
has a homogeneous basis
\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}}\mid{\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n},\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda),\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}
. Fix a multicharge
(\kappa_{\ell_{k}},\kappa_{\ell_{k-1}},\ldots,\kappa_{2},\kappa_{1})
corresponding
\Lambda^{(k)}
. For any homogeneous element
r\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
, there exists
c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\in\mathbb{Z}
with
\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}
such that

\displaystyle r+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\sum_{\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}=\sum_{\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\hat{\psi}_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle r-\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}.

But as
r
is a homogeneous element which is not in
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
, we must have
r-\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}=0
, i.e.
r=\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}
with
\res(\hat{\mathsf{t}})=\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}
. This shows that
r
belongs to the span of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
. Hence
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
is spanned by
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
.

Next we will prove that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is linearly independent. Suppose
S_{\alpha}
is a finite subset of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
. Write
m_{S_{\alpha}}=\max\mathinner{\{\,{\deg(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}})}\mid{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}}\,\}}
. By
subsection 5.2
there exists
k
such that
m^{\Lambda^{(k)}}_{\alpha}>m_{S_{\alpha}}
. Hence
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\not\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
for any
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}
. This means that for any
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}
,
\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
is nonzero. As by the definition,
\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}}\mid{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}}\,\}}
is a subset of the basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
. We have
\sum_{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
if and only if
\sum_{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}=0
if and only if all
c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}=0
. But
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\not\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
for any
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}
, the above result yields that
\sum_{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in S_{\alpha}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}=0
if and only if
c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}=0
. This shows that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is linearly independent. Hence
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
. ∎

Notice that in the definition of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
, it is well-defined for any inverse multicharge sequence
\kappa
corresponds to
\Lambda^{\infty}
. Hence for any weight
\Lambda
with
\ell=l(\Lambda)
, by the definition of the standard sequence, we can set
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda
. Therefore, we obtain a subset of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
:

\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}=\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}}\mid{\text{$\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}$ with $l(\hat{\lambda})\leq\ell$},\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda}),\res(\hat{\mathsf{t}})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}.

Corollary 5.16
.

Suppose
\Lambda
is a weight with level
\ell
and
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence with
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda
. Then

\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}\backslash\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}=\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}}\mid{\text{$\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}$ with $l(\hat{\lambda})>\ell=l(\Lambda)$},\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda}),\res(\hat{\mathsf{t}})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}

is a basis of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

Proof.

By
subsection 5.1
,
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
has a basis
\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}}\mid{\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n},\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda),\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}
. It is easy to see that when
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda
,

\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}}\mid{\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n},\mathsf{s},\mathsf{t}\in\Std(\lambda),\res(\mathsf{t})\in I^{\alpha}}\,\}}=\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}=\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}+N_{n}^{\Lambda}}\mid{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in\mathscr{B}_{\Lambda}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}}\,\}}.

So for
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}
, we must have
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\not\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

Now suppose
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}\backslash\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}
. Then
\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
with
l(\hat{\lambda})>\ell
. By the definition it is obvious that
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
when
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda
. Then
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
is spanned by
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}\backslash\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}
.
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a basis implies the linearly independence of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}\backslash\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}
. So
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}\backslash\mathscr{B}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}_{\Lambda}
is a basis of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
. ∎

Recall for any
\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
with
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
, we define
\psi^{*}_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}=\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}
. By
subsection 5.3
,
*
can be defined to be a linear bijection from
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
to
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
. The next Corollary is straightforward by
subsection 5.3
.

Corollary 5.17
.

Suppose
*\,{:}\,\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
is defined as above. Then it can be restricted to a linear bijection
*\,{:}\,N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}\!\longrightarrow\!N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
.

Now we can prove the main result of this section.

Proposition 5.18
.

Suppose
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence and
\alpha\in Q_{+}
. The set
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
.

Proof.

Recall
subsection 2.2
gives the definition of graded cellular basis.
subsection 5.3
shows that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a homogeneous basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
. To prove the Theorem we need to establish properties
2.2
(b) and
2.2
(c) of
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
.

Suppose
a
is an element of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
and
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\in\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
with
\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})
. We can write
a=\sum_{i\in\mathbb{N}}c_{i}a_{i}
where
c_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}
and
a_{i}
are homogeneous elements in
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
with
\deg(a_{i})=i
. Define
d_{1}=\deg(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}})
and
d_{2}=\max\{i\ |\ c_{i}\neq 0\}
. By
subsection 5.2
there exists
k
such that
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}>\max\{d_{1},d_{2},d_{1}+d_{2}\}
. This means that
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}
,
a
and
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}a
are not elements of
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
. This means that
\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}=\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
,
a+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
and
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}a+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
are nonzero elements of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
. By
subsection 5.1
and because
t
is a bijection,

\displaystyle\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}(a+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})=(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})(a+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})=\sum_{\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\lambda)}c_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{v}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathsf{u},\mathsf{v}\in\Std(\mu)\\
\mu\rhd\lambda\end{subarray}}c_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}}

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}a+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}=\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{\mathsf{u}},\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\mu})\\
\hat{\mu}\rhd\hat{\lambda}\end{subarray}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}

\displaystyle\Rightarrow

\displaystyle\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}a-(\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{\mathsf{u}},\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\mu})\\
\hat{\mu}\rhd\hat{\lambda}\end{subarray}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}.

Since the left hand side of the above equation is homogeneous to
d_{1}+d_{2}
and
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}>d_{1}+d_{2}
, we see that

\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}a=\sum_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})}c_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\hat{\mathsf{u}},\hat{\mathsf{v}}\in\Std(\hat{\mu})\\
\hat{\mu}\rhd\hat{\lambda}\end{subarray}}c_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}.

which shows that
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
satisfies
2.2
(b).

For
2.2
(c), choose arbitrary
\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}},\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}\in\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
. Suppose
\deg(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}})=k_{1}
and
\deg(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})=d_{2}
. By
subsection 5.2
we can choose
k
so that
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}>\max\{k_{1},k_{2},k_{1}+k_{2}\}
. Then by
subsection 5.3
,

\displaystyle(\psi_{\mathsf{s}\mathsf{t}}\psi_{\mathsf{u}\mathsf{v}})^{*}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle((\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}))^{*}=(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})^{*}=(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})^{*}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}},

\displaystyle\psi_{\mathsf{v}\mathsf{u}}\psi_{\mathsf{t}\mathsf{s}}

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\hat{\mathsf{u}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}})=\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\hat{\mathsf{u}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}+N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}},

which implies that
(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})^{*}-\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\hat{\mathsf{u}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}=N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}
. Then because
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(k)}}>k_{1}+k_{2}
,
(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})^{*}-\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{v}}\hat{\mathsf{u}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}=0
, i.e.
(\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}})^{*}=\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{u}}\hat{\mathsf{v}}}^{*}\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{t}}\hat{\mathsf{s}}}^{*}
. Because
*
is a linear bijection and
\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
is a basis of
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
, this shows that
*\,{:}\,\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}\!\longrightarrow\!\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
is an anti-isomorphism. Hence
*
satisfies
2.2
(c). This completes the proof.∎

Combining the above two Propositions and
subsection 5.3
we can get the following results.

Theorem 5.19
.

For any standard sequence
\Lambda^{\infty}
, the set

\mathscr{B}_{n}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}=\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}}\mid{\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n},\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})}\,\}}

is a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
.

Proof.

By definition we have
\mathscr{B}_{n}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_{+}}\mathscr{B}_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{\infty}}
and
\mathscr{R}_{n}=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in Q_{+}}\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
. By the relations of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
we see that
\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
are subalgebras. The Theorem follows by
subsection 5.3
straightforward. ∎

Corollary 5.20
.

Suppose
\Lambda
is a weight with level
\ell
and
\Lambda^{\infty}
is a standard sequence with
\Lambda^{(1)}=\Lambda
. Then

\mathinner{\{\,{\psi_{\hat{\mathsf{s}}\hat{\mathsf{t}}}}\mid{\text{$\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}$ with $l(\hat{\lambda})>\ell=l(\Lambda)$},\hat{\mathsf{s}},\hat{\mathsf{t}}\in\Std(\hat{\lambda})}\,\}}

is a basis of
N_{n}^{\Lambda}
.

5.4. Graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules

subsection 5.3
gives a graded cellular basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
. Graham and Lehrer
[
7
]
described a complete set of irreducible representations of any finite dimensional cellular algebra, however, their results do not apply to
\mathscr{R}_{n}
because it is an infinite dimensional algebra. In this subsection we use Graham and Lehrer’s results to construct a complete set of graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. The graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules have been desccribed by Brundan and Kleshchev
[
4
, Theorem 5.19]
. See
subsection 5.4
for more detials.

First we need to state some properties of the simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. We start by showing that the graded dimension of an simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module is bounded below.

Lemma 5.21
.

Suppose
r\in\mathscr{R}_{n}
is a homogeneous element. Then
\deg(r)\geq-n(n-1)
.

Proof.

By (
2.40
) we have the following basis of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
:

\mathinner{\{\,{\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{y}_{1}^{\ell_{1}}\hat{y}_{2}^{\ell_{2}}\ldots\hat{y}_{n}^{\ell_{n}}\hat{\psi}_{w}}\mid{\mathbf{i}\in I^{n},w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n},\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{n}\geq 0}\,\}}.

If
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
,
w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
and
\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ldots,\ell_{n}\geq 0
, then

\displaystyle\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{y}_{1}^{\ell_{1}}\hat{y}_{2}^{\ell_{2}}\ldots\hat{y}_{n}^{\ell_{n}}\hat{\psi}_{w})

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{y}_{1}^{\ell_{1}}\hat{y}_{2}^{\ell_{2}}\ldots\hat{y}_{n}^{\ell_{n}})+\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{\psi}_{w})

\displaystyle=

\displaystyle 2(\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}+\ldots+\ell_{n})+\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{\psi}_{w})

\displaystyle\geq

\displaystyle\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{\psi}_{w}).

As
w\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}
, we have
l(w)\leq\frac{n(n-1)}{2}
and by definition,
\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{\psi}_{r}\geq-2
for any
r
and
\mathbf{i}\in I^{n}
. Therefore

\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{\psi}_{w})\geq-2\times\frac{n(n-1)}{2}=-n(n-1).

Hence
\deg(\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\hat{y}_{1}^{\ell_{1}}\hat{y}_{2}^{\ell_{2}}\ldots\hat{y}_{n}^{\ell_{n}}\hat{\psi}_{w})\geq-n(n-1)
. This completes the proof. ∎

Recall that for
|\alpha|=\sum_{i\in I}a_{i}
and
\hat{e}_{\alpha}=\sum_{\mathbf{i}\in I^{\alpha}}\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})\in\mathscr{R}_{n}
.

Lemma 5.22
.

Suppose
S
is a simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module. Then there exists
\alpha\in Q_{+}
with
|\alpha|=n
such that for any
\beta\in Q_{+}
with
|\beta|=n
,
\hat{e}_{\beta}S=\delta_{\alpha\beta}S
.

Proof.

Suppose
S
is a simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module. Because
1=\sum_{\mathbf{j}\in I^{n}}\hat{e}(\mathbf{j})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\in Q_{+}\\
|\beta|=n\end{subarray}}\hat{e}_{\beta}
, we can write
S=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\in Q_{+}\\
|\beta|=n\end{subarray}}\hat{e}_{\beta}S
. Suppose
\hat{e}_{\alpha}S\neq 0
for some
\alpha\in Q_{+}
. Choose any nonzero element
s\in S
and
\beta\in Q_{+}
with
\beta\neq\alpha
. By
subsection 5.1
,
\hat{e}_{\alpha}\mathscr{R}_{n}\hat{e}_{\beta}=0
. So we must have
\hat{e}_{\beta}{\cdot}s=0
. Hence
\hat{e}_{\beta}S=0
. Therefore
S=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\beta\in Q_{+}\\
|\beta|=n\end{subarray}}\hat{e}_{\beta}S=\hat{e}_{\alpha}S
. This completes the proof. ∎

It is well-known that the irreducible representations of the affine Hecke algebra are finite dimensional as, by Bernstein, the affine Hecke algebra is finite dimensional over its centre. See for example, Proposition 4.1 and Corollary 4.2 of Grojnowski
[
8
]
, or Proposition 2.12 of Khovanov-Lauda
[
13
]
. The next Proposition gives a different approach.

Proposition 5.23
.

Suppose
S
is a graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module and
\alpha\in Q_{+}
is such that
\hat{e}_{\beta}S=\delta_{\alpha\beta}S
for
\beta\in Q_{+}
. If
\Lambda\in P_{+}
with
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}>n(n-1)
, then
S
is isomorphic to a graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-module.

Proof.

By
subsection 5.4
there exists
\alpha\in Q_{+}
such that
\hat{e}_{\beta}S=\delta_{\alpha\beta}S
for
\beta\in Q_{+}
. Then we choose an arbitrary nonzero homogeneous element
s\in S
and suppose
\deg(s)=d
. Now for any nonzero homogeneous element
t\in S
, because
S
is simple, there exists a homogeneous element
a\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
such that
t=a{\cdot}s
. Therefore

\deg(t)=\deg(a{\cdot}s)=\deg(a)+\deg(s)\geq d-n(n-1)

where by
subsection 5.4
we have
\deg(a)\geq-n(n-1)
. So for any homogeneous nonzero element
t\in S
, we have

\deg(t)\geq d-n(n-1).

(5.24)

Similarly, since for any nonzero homogeneous element
t\in\mathscr{R}_{n}
there exists a homogeneous element
a\in\mathscr{R}_{\alpha}
such that
s=a{\cdot}t
, we have

\deg(t)\leq d+n(n-1).

(5.25)

Combining (
5.24
) and (
5.25
), we have
|\deg(s)-\deg(t)|\leq n(n-1)
for any nonzero homogeneous element
t\in S
. Because
s
is chosen arbitrarily, we have

|\deg(s)-\deg(t)|\leq n(n-1)

(5.26)

for any nonzero homogeneous elements
s,t\in S
.

Suppose
\Lambda\in P_{+}
with
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}>n(n-1)
. For any homogeneous element
a\in N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}
and
t\in S
, we have
a{\cdot}t=0
because
\deg(a{\cdot}t)-\deg(t)=\deg(a)>n(n-1)
and (
5.26
).

For any
s\in S
, we can define a map
f\,{:}\,\mathscr{R}_{n}\!\longrightarrow\!S
by sending
a
to
a{\cdot}s
. It is a homomorphism and it is obvious that
N_{\alpha}^{\Lambda}\subseteq\text{ker}f
. If
\beta\in Q_{+}
and
\beta\neq\alpha
, then by
subsection 5.4
we have
\hat{e}_{\beta}{\cdot}s=0
. Therefore
N_{\beta}^{\Lambda}\subseteq\text{ker}f
. Hence
N_{n}^{\Lambda}\subseteq\text{ker}f
. Therefore we can consider
S
as a simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}/N_{n}^{\Lambda}
-module, i.e.
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-module. This completes the proof. ∎

Corollary 5.27
.

Suppose
S
is a simple graded
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module. Then
S
is finite-dimensional.

Building on Ariki’s
[
1
]
work in the ungraded case, Hu and Mathas
[
9
]
constructed all graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules in the sense of Graham-Lehrer
[
7
]
. They proved that, up to shift, graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules are labeled by the
Kleshchev multipartitions
of
n
, which were introduced by Ariki and Mathas
[
2
]
. Readers may also refer to Brundan and Kleshchev
[
4
, (3.27)]
(where they are called
restricted multipartitions
).

Suppose
\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\lambda^{(2)},\ldots,\lambda^{(\ell)})\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
and we consider the Young diagram
[\lambda]
. Let
\gamma=(r,c,l)
be a node in the Young diagram with residue
i
, i.e.
i\equiv r-c+\kappa_{l}\pmod{e}
. Then
\gamma
is an addable
i
-node if
\gamma\not\in[\lambda]
and
[\lambda]\cup\{\gamma\}
is the Young diagram of a multipartition, and
\gamma
is a removable
i
-node if
\gamma\in[\lambda]
and
[\lambda]\backslash\{\gamma\}
is the Young diagram of a multipartition.

For each
\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
, we read all addable and removable
i
-nodes in the following order: we start with the first row of
\lambda^{(1)}
, and then read rows in
\lambda^{(1)}
downward. We then read the first row of
\lambda^{(2)}
, and repeat the same procedure, until we finish reading all rows of
\lambda
. We write
A
for an addable
i
-node, and
R
for a removable
i
-node. Hence we get a sequence of
A
and
R
. We then delete
RA
as many as possible. For example, if we have a sequence
RARARRAAARRAR
, the resulting sequence will be
--------AR--R
. The node corresponding to the leftmost R is the
good
i
-node
.

The Kleshchev multipartition can then be defined recursively as follows.

Definition 5.28
.

[
1
, Definition 2.3]

We declare that
\emptyset
is Kelshchev. Assume that we have already defined the set of Kleshchev multipartitions up to size
n-1
. Let
\lambda
be a multipartition of
n
. We say that
\lambda
is a Kleshchev multipartition if there is a good node
\gamma
in
[\lambda]
such that if
[\mu]=[\lambda]\backslash\{\gamma\}
then
\mu
is a Kleshchev multipartition.

Let
\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{0}
be the set of Kleshchev multipartitions in
\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
. Let
S^{\lambda}
be the cell module of
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
(it is called the
Specht module
in
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
), which was introduced in subsection 1.2, and
D^{\lambda}=S^{\lambda}/\text{rad }S^{\lambda}
. Hu-Mathas
[
9
, Corollary 5.11]
gave a set of complete non-isomorphic graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules. We note that the graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules were first constructed by Brundan and Kleshchev
[
4
, Theorem 4.11]
giving the same classification but without using cellular algebra techniques.

Theorem 5.29
.

The set
\mathinner{\{\,{D^{\lambda}\langle k\rangle}\mid{\lambda\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{0},k\in\mathbb{Z}}\,\}}
is a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic graded simple
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules.

We consider
S^{\lambda}
and
D^{\lambda}\langle k\rangle
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. The actions of
\hat{e}(\mathbf{i})
,
\hat{y}_{r}
and
\hat{\psi}_{s}
on
S^{\lambda}
and
D^{\lambda}\langle k\rangle
are the same as the actions of
e(\mathbf{i})
,
y_{r}
and
\psi_{s}
. Therefore
D^{\lambda}\langle k\rangle
is a simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module. Hence the modules in
subsection 5.4
are a set of simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

The next Lemma is straightforward by the definition of
D^{\lambda}
.

Lemma 5.30
.

Suppose
\lambda,\mu\in\mathscr{P}^{\Lambda}_{n}
. Then
D^{\lambda}\cong D^{\mu}
as
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
-modules if and only if
D^{\lambda}\cong D^{\mu}
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

Now we can classify all graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. Following the definitions in Section 1.2, for each
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
we define the cell module
S^{\hat{\lambda}}
of
\mathscr{R}_{n}
, which we also call a
Specht module
, associated with a bilinear form
\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle
. Then we define
\text{rad }S^{\hat{\lambda}}
and hence the graded simple module
D^{\hat{\lambda}}=S^{\hat{\lambda}}/\text{rad }S^{\hat{\lambda}}
.

Lemma 5.31
.

Suppose
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
and
\mu=p_{k}(\hat{\lambda})
for some
k\geq l(\hat{\lambda})
. Then
S^{\mu}\cong S^{\hat{\lambda}}
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

Proof.

This is trivial given the definition of Specht modules in
\mathscr{R}_{n}
and
\mathscr{R}^{\Lambda}_{n}
. ∎

The next Corollary is straightforward by
subsection 5.4
and
subsection 5.4
.

Corollary 5.32
.

Suppose
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
and
\mu=p_{k}(\hat{\lambda})
for some
k\geq l(\hat{\lambda})
. Then
D^{\mu}\cong D^{\hat{\lambda}}
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

Hence we can prove the following Lemma.

Lemma 5.33
.

Suppose
\hat{\lambda},\hat{\mu}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
. Then
D^{\hat{\lambda}}\cong D^{\hat{\mu}}
if and only if
\hat{\lambda}=\hat{\mu}
.

Proof.

The if part is trivial. Now suppose
D^{\hat{\lambda}}\cong D^{\hat{\mu}}
. Choose
k>\max\{l(\hat{\lambda}),l(\hat{\mu})\}
and set
\nu=p_{k}(\hat{\lambda})
and
\sigma=p_{k}(\hat{\mu})
. Then by
subsection 5.4
we have
D^{\nu}\cong D^{\sigma}
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. Then
subsection 5.4
and
subsection 5.4
implies
\nu=\sigma
. Therefore by the definition of
k
we have
\hat{\lambda}=\hat{\mu}
. This completes the proof. ∎

Now we extend the Kleshchev multipartitions to affine multipartitions. Define
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
to be an
affine Kleshchev multipartition
if
\lambda
is a Kleshchev multipartition. Let
\mathscr{P}_{0}^{\kappa}
be the set of all affine Kleshchev multipartitions in
\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
. We can now give a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

Theorem 5.34
.

The set
\mathinner{\{\,{D^{\hat{\lambda}}\langle k\rangle}\mid{\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}_{0}^{\kappa},k\in\mathbb{Z}}\,\}}
is a complete set of pairwise non-isomorphic graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

Proof.

By the definition of (affine) Kleshchev multipartitions,
[
9
, Corollary 5.11]
and
subsection 5.4
,
D^{\hat{\lambda}}\langle k\rangle\cong D^{\lambda}\langle k\rangle\neq 0
if and only if
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}_{0}^{\kappa}
.

Suppose
S
is a graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-module. By
subsection 5.4
there exists
\alpha\in Q_{+}
such that
\hat{e}_{\beta}S=\delta_{\alpha\beta}S
for
\beta\in Q_{+}
. Then by
subsection 5.2
we can choose
i
such that
m_{\alpha}^{\Lambda^{(i)}}>n(n-1)
and hence by
subsection 5.4
,
S
is isomorphic to a graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda^{(i)}}
-module. Therefore, by
subsection 5.4
there exist some
\mu\in\mathscr{P}_{n}^{\Lambda^{(i)}}
and
k\in\mathbb{Z}
such that
S\cong D^{\mu}\langle k\rangle
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}^{\Lambda^{(i)}}
-modules, and hence as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. Suppose
l(\mu)=\ell
. We can choose
\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}^{\kappa}_{n}
such that
p_{\ell}(\hat{\lambda})=\mu
with
l(\hat{\lambda})\leq\ell
. By
subsection 5.4
we have
D^{\hat{\lambda}}\cong D^{\mu}
as
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. Therefore,
S\cong D^{\hat{\lambda}}\langle k\rangle
. So

\mathinner{\{\,{D^{\hat{\lambda}}\langle k\rangle}\mid{\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}_{0}^{\kappa},k\in\mathbb{Z}}\,\}}

is a complete set of graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules.

By
subsection 5.4
, the set
\mathinner{\{\,{D^{\hat{\lambda}}\langle k\rangle}\mid{\hat{\lambda}\in\mathscr{P}_{0}^{\kappa},k\in\mathbb{Z}}\,\}}
is a set of pairwise non-isomorphic graded
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules. This completes the proof. ∎

Remark 5.35
.

Ariki-Mathas
[
2
]
showed that the simple
H_{n}
-modules are indexed by aperiodic multisegments. Khovanov and Lauda
[
13
,
12
]
also give a classification of the graded simple
\mathscr{R}_{n}
-modules for KLR algebras of arbitrary type. Interested readers may also refer to
[
15
]
,
[
4
]
,
[
16
]
,
[
18
]
,
[
25
]
,
[
11
]
and
[
21
]
. As far as we are aware the construction and classification in
subsection 5.4
is new.
